claim: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the most common type of birth defect affecting 0.8% of human live births.
source: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the most common type of birth defect affecting 0.8% of human live births (Fahed et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fahed et al., 2013

claim: Current genomic technologies have provided a genetic diagnosis for only 11% of CHD probands.
source: Although genetic factors play a significant role in the development of CHD, current genomic technologies, including exome sequencing and SNP arrays, have provided a genetic diagnosis for only 11% of the probands (Gelb et al., 2013), highlighting the crucial role of non-genetic contributors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gelb et al., 2013

claim: Maternal hyperglycemia is associated with a 2–5-fold increase in CHD independent of genetic contributors.
source: Among the non-genetic factors that influence the fetal heart, maternal hyperglycemia is the most common medical condition, associated with a 2–5-fold increase in CHD independent of genetic contributors (Centers for Disease Control, 1990; Simeone et al., 2015; Yogev and Visser, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Centers for Disease Control, 1990; Simeone et al., 2015; Yogev and Visser, 2009

claim: hESC-CMs differentiated in monolayer in chemically defined conditions reproducibly yield ~90% of MF20+ cardiomyocytes at day 14.
source: hESC-CMs were differentiated in monolayer in a chemically defined condition, reproducibly yielding ~90% of MF20+ cardiomyocytes at day 14 with multiple cell lines including WA09 (H9) and UCLA4 hESCs (Figure 1A–C) (Arshi et al., 2013; Minami et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arshi et al., 2013; Minami et al., 2012 and data shown in Figure 1A-C

claim: hESC-CMs start to beat synchronously at around day 6–7.
source: hESC-CMs start to beat synchronously at around day 6–7 in our system.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation in the described system

claim: Glucose dose-dependently suppresses the expression of TNNT2, NKX2-5, and PPARGC1A in hESC-CMs.
source: Interestingly, glucose dose-dependently suppressed the expression of TNNT2 (a cardiac marker), NKX2-5 (a cardiac marker), and PPARGC1A (a mitochondrial marker) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Genes related to cardiac muscle and function are enriched in hESC-CMs in low glucose medium.
source: Gene expression profiling by RNA-seq revealed that genes that are related to cardiac muscle and function are enriched in hESC-CMs in low glucose medium, and that genes that are associated with mitosis and cell cycle are enriched in the high-glucose group genome-wide (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; GSE84814).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, deposited as GSE84814

claim: Genes associated with mitosis and cell cycle are enriched in hESC-CMs cultured in high-glucose medium.
source: Gene expression profiling by RNA-seq revealed that genes that are related to cardiac muscle and function are enriched in hESC-CMs in low glucose medium, and that genes that are associated with mitosis and cell cycle are enriched in the high-glucose group genome-wide (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; GSE84814).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, deposited as GSE84814

claim: Low glucose decreases mitotic activity in hESC-CMs at day 28 without affecting viability.
source: Low glucose decreased mitotic activity at day 28 without affecting the viability of hESC-CMs (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by pH3 staining and EdU flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and 2E

claim: hESC-CMs cultured in low glucose media have increased mitochondrial contents.
source: MitoTracker staining and flow cytometry analyses revealed that hESC-CMs cultured in low glucose media have increased mitochondrial contents and inter-myofibrillar distribution of mitochondria, characteristic of differentiated cardiomyocytes (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by MitoTracker staining and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F and 2G

claim: Addition of 2-DG induces higher levels of MitoTracker and MF20 expression even in the presence of 5 mM or 25 mM glucose.
source: Addition of 2-DG (2-deoxy-D-glucose), a competitive inhibitor of glucose phosphorylation, induced higher levels of MitoTracker and MF20 expression even in the presence of 5 mM or 25 mM glucose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the effect is specific to glucose and not to changes in osmotic pressure.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Flow cytometry shows a significant increase in cell size under glucose-restricted conditions.
source: Consistently, flow cytometry showed a significant increase in cell size under glucose-restricted conditions (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2I

claim: Mitochondria in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs are more elongated.
source: Immunofluorescent staining revealed that mitochondria in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs are more elongated (Figure 3A), and flow cytometry analysis revealed that the level of JC-1 aggregation is significantly higher in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs cultured in both regular 0.9 mM and 10 mM pyruvate conditions. (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent staining shown in Figure 3A

claim: The level of JC-1 aggregation is significantly higher in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs.
source: Immunofluorescent staining revealed that mitochondria in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs are more elongated (Figure 3A), and flow cytometry analysis revealed that the level of JC-1 aggregation is significantly higher in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs cultured in both regular 0.9 mM and 10 mM pyruvate conditions. (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: In hESC-CMs differentiated in standard 25 mM glucose, addition of pyruvate evokes intracellular lactate accumulation.
source: In hESC-CMs differentiated in standard 25 mM glucose, bath-applied lactate (4 mM) caused a rapid increase in intracellular lactate (measured as a decrease FRET ratio), demonstrating the efficacy of the probe. Subsequent addition of pyruvate evoked a similar but smaller elevation of intracellular lactate.
evidence: Supported by Laconic FRET measurements described in the text and shown in Figure 3C

claim: Addition of 4 mM pyruvate to glucose-reduced hESC-CMs does not cause intracellular lactate accumulation.
source: By contrast, addition of 4 mM pyruvate to glucose-reduced hESC-CMs did not cause intracellular lactate accumulation, and addition of NaCN in the presence of pyruvate resulted in a substantial increase in lactate level.
evidence: Supported by Laconic FRET measurements described in the text and shown in Figure 3C

claim: ATP-linked respiration is elevated in hESC-CMs cultured in no glucose condition.
source: Although base-line mitochondrial respiration was not changed (Figure 3E), ATP-linked respiration was elevated in the no glucose condition (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse XF24 analyzer data shown in Figure 3F and 3G

claim: Glucose-reduced hESC-CMs demonstrate substantially larger maximum respiration capacity.
source: Glucose-reduced hESC-CMs also demonstrated substantially larger maximum respiration capacity, as indicated by the response to FCCP (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse XF24 analyzer data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The maximum upstroke (Vmax) of Ca2+ transients is significantly faster in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs.
source: Although the peak amplitude of the transient (ΔF/F0) did not show a significant difference, the maximum upstroke (Vmax) was significantly faster and the time to 50% decay was significantly shorter in the glucose-reduced group (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ transient assay data shown in Figure 3I

claim: The time to 50% decay of Ca2+ transients is significantly shorter in glucose-reduced hESC-CMs.
source: Although the peak amplitude of the transient (ΔF/F0) did not show a significant difference, the maximum upstroke (Vmax) was significantly faster and the time to 50% decay was significantly shorter in the glucose-reduced group (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by Ca2+ transient assay data shown in Figure 3I

claim: hESC-CMs cultured in the absence of glucose display a significant increase in dV/dtmax of field potential.
source: Compared with hESC-CMs cultured in 25 mM glucose, those hESC-CMs cultured in the absence of glucose displayed a significant increase in dV/dtmax (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by multi-electrode array data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Both average maximum contraction speed and average maximum relaxation speed are higher in hESC-CMs cultured in 0 mM glucose.
source: Both average maximum contraction speed and average maximum relaxation speed were higher in those hESC-CMs cultured in 0 mM glucose (Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by digital image correlation data shown in Figure 3J

claim: Glucose deprivation results in a significant decrease in the levels of metabolites in purine metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, the PPP, the hexosamine pathway, and glycolysis.
source: Mass spectrometry revealed that glucose deprivation resulted in a significant decrease in the levels of the metabolites in purine metabolism, pyrimidine metabolism, the PPP, the hexosamine pathway, and glycolysis, whereas lipid precursors, amino acids, glutamine, and glutamate, as well as urea cycle metabolites, were not significantly affected (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: ATP levels are not significantly different under glucose-restricted conditions.
source: ATP levels were not significantly different under glucose-restricted conditions (Figure 4B), neither were any specific stress pathways significantly increased when examined by RNA-seq, suggesting that the cells were not energy-starved in the absence of glucose in the cell culture media.
evidence: Supported by ATP measurement data shown in Figure 4B and RNA-seq analysis

claim: 2-DG dose-dependently abolishes the glucose-dependent inhibition of TNNT2 and NKX2-5 mRNA levels in hESC-CM.
source: Consistent with flow cytometry for MitoTracker and MF20 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), 2-DG dose-dependently abolished the glucose-dependent inhibition of TNNT2 and NKX2-5 mRNA levels in hESC-CM (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A

claim: 3PO does not affect the level of hESC-CM maturity at any concentration of glucose.
source: 3PO (3-[3-pyridinyl]-1-[4-pyridinyl]-2-propen-1-one), an inhibitor of the phosphofructokinase PFKFB3 (which is a regulator of PFK1), did not affect the level of hESC-CM maturity at any concentration of glucose (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B

claim: Sodium oxamate does not block the inhibitory effect of glucose on hESC-CM maturation.
source: Consistently, sodium oxamate (a lactate dehydrogenase [LDH] inhibitor) did not block the inhibitory effect of glucose (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C

claim: 6AN and DHEA, both inhibitors of G6PD, recapitulate the effect of glucose reduction on hESC-CM maturation.
source: Interestingly, however, 6AN (6-[cyclohexa-2,5-dien-1-ylideneamino] naphthalene-2-sulfonate) and DHEA (didehydroepiandrosterone), both inhibitors of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) in the oxidative arm of the PPP, recapitulated glucose reduction (Figure 4G and H, Figure 4—figure supplement 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4G, 4H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4D-E

claim: The pentose phosphate pathway plays a critical role in the glucose-dependent inhibition of cardiac maturation.
source: As summarized in Figure 4—figure supplement 3, our chemical inhibitor screening suggests that the PPP plays a critical role in the inhibition of cardiac maturation and that blocking this pathway by either use of chemical inhibitors or glucose deprivation induces cardiac maturation.
evidence: Supported by chemical inhibitor screening data summarized in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Uridine restores cell proliferation even in low-glucose conditions.
source: In our hESC-CM culture system, uridine restored cell proliferation even in low-glucose conditions (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by pH3 staining data shown in Figure 5A and 5B

claim: Uridine dose-dependently reduces the level of TNNT2 even in glucose-deprived conditions.
source: Interestingly, uridine dose-dependently reduced the level of TNNT2 even in glucose-deprived conditions (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that glucose-mediated inhibition of cardiac maturation is dependent on the supply of nucleotides and not of NADPH.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Addition of excess thymidine increases the expression of TNNT2 and NKX2-5 in hESC-CMs.
source: When excess thymidine was added to hESC-CMs, the expression of TNNT2 and NKX2-5 were increased (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Hydroxyurea dose-dependently induces the expression of TNNT2 and NKX2-5 in hESC-CMs.
source: Consistent with the results from thymidine block, HU dose-dependently induced the expression of TNNT2 and NKX2-5 (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: RNAi-based knockdown of RRM2B results in a significant increase in TNNT2 expression level, even in the presence of 25 mM glucose.
source: RNAi-based knockdown of RRM2B, a key subunit of RNR, also resulted in a significant increase in TNNT2 expression level, even in the presence of 25 mM glucose (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown and qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Neither CDK4/6 inhibitor nor paclitaxel induces cardiac maturation in hESC-CMs.
source: Interestingly, neither CDK4/6 inhibitor nor paclitaxel induced cardiac maturation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B

claim: Normalized cardiac 18F-FDG accumulation progressively and rapidly decreases from E10.5 to P7.
source: Interestingly, the normalized cardiac accumulation progressively and rapidly decreased from E10.5 to P7, with 0.11% and 0.05% 18F-FDG uptake in P1 and P7 hearts, respectively, compared to E10.5 hearts (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by 18F-FDG PET/CT measurements shown in Figure 6

claim: Cardiac glucose uptake becomes significantly restricted during late gestational and early postnatal stages.
source: These data suggest that cardiac glucose uptake becomes significantly restricted during late gestational and early postnatal stages, creating an intracellular glucose deprivation condition during natural in vivo development.
evidence: Inferred from 18F-FDG uptake data shown in Figure 6

claim: The average blood-glucose levels of Akita mothers are significantly higher than those of sex-matched control littermates (215 ± 84 vs 71 ± 12 mg/dl, p<0.0005).
source: In the C57BL/6 background, the average blood-glucose levels of the Akita mothers that we used were significantly higher than those of sex-matched control littermates (215 ± 84 vs 71 ± 12 mg/dl, respectively; p<0.0005).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements in the Akita mouse model

claim: The number of cardiomyocytes in S phase is significantly higher at both E16.5 and P0 in embryos from diabetic pregnancies.
source: As shown in Figure 7B and C, the number of cardiomyocytes in S phase was significantly higher at both E16.5 and P0 in the diabetes group.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data shown in Figure 7B and 7C

claim: The number of phosphorylated histone H3-positive cardiomyocytes is higher at E16.5 in embryos from diabetic pregnancies.
source: Histological analyses showed that the number of phosphorylated histone H3-positive cardiomyocytes (pH3+/Tnnt2+) is higher at E16.5 in the embryos from diabetic pregnancies (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D and 7E

claim: The level of Tnnt2 expression is significantly lower in hearts from diabetic pregnancies.
source: The level of Tnnt2 expression was significantly lower in the hearts from the diabetic pregnancies (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F

claim: The thickness of left and right ventricular free walls is significantly increased in hearts from diabetic pregnancies at P1.
source: Although heart weight/body weight ratio did not show a difference in our mouse model, the thickness of left and right ventricular free walls was significantly increased in the hearts from diabetic pregnancies at P1 (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Cardiomyocyte size measured by flow cytometry is significantly smaller in the diabetic pregnancy group.
source: Consistently, the cardiomyocyte size measured by flow cytometry was significantly smaller in the diabetic pregnancy group (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7H

claim: Overproliferation and/or delayed maturation underlie the pathological mechanism of cardiomyopathy associated with diabetic pregnancy.
source: These data suggest that overproliferation and/or delayed maturation underlie the pathological mechanism of cardiomyopathy associated with diabetic pregnancy.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on increased proliferation and decreased maturation in diabetic pregnancy model

claim: Glucose dose-dependently inhibits cardiac maturation in hESC-CMs.
source: In summary, we investigated the role of glucose in cardiac formation, and discovered (1) that glucose dose-dependently inhibits cardiac maturation in hESC-CMs
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript including Figures 2 and 3

claim: The maturation-inhibitory effect of glucose is dependent on nucleotide biosynthesis via the PPP.
source: In summary, we investigated the role of glucose in cardiac formation, and discovered (1) that glucose dose-dependently inhibits cardiac maturation in hESC-CMs, (2) that the maturation-inhibitory effect is dependent on nucleotide biosynthesis via the PPP
evidence: Supported by chemical inhibitor screening and nucleotide supplementation experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: The developing heart accomplishes intracellular glucose starvation by limiting glucose uptake in late gestational stages during normal embryogenesis.
source: In summary, we investigated the role of glucose in cardiac formation, and discovered (1) that glucose dose-dependently inhibits cardiac maturation in hESC-CMs, (2) that the maturation-inhibitory effect is dependent on nucleotide biosynthesis via the PPP, (3) that the developing heart accomplishes intracellular glucose starvation by limiting glucose uptake in late gestational stages during normal embryogenesis
evidence: Supported by 18F-FDG uptake measurements shown in Figure 6

claim: Perturbation of environmental glucose level in diabetic pregnancy affects natural cardiomyocyte maturation in vivo.
source: In summary, we investigated the role of glucose in cardiac formation, and discovered (1) that glucose dose-dependently inhibits cardiac maturation in hESC-CMs, (2) that the maturation-inhibitory effect is dependent on nucleotide biosynthesis via the PPP, (3) that the developing heart accomplishes intracellular glucose starvation by limiting glucose uptake in late gestational stages during normal embryogenesis, and (4) that perturbation of the environmental glucose level in diabetic pregnancy affects natural cardiomyocyte maturation in vivo.
evidence: Supported by Akita mouse model data shown in Figure 7

claim: Cardiomyocytes switch their main energy substrate from glucose to fatty acids shortly after birth.
source: Cardiomyocytes switch their main energy substrate from glucose (or other carbohydrates) to fatty acids shortly after birth.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about cardiac metabolism

claim: A drastic suppression of glucose uptake occurs during gestational stages, long before the metabolic switch after birth.
source: However, our study has revealed that a drastic suppression of glucose uptake occurs during gestational stages, long before the metabolic switch after birth (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by 18F-FDG uptake data shown in Figure 6 (note: text says Figure 5 but refers to Figure 6 data)

claim: Glucose deprivation induces cardiac maturation at genetic, morphological, metabolic, electrophysiological and biomechanical levels.
source: The results suggest that glucose deprivation induces cardiac maturation at genetic, morphological, metabolic, electrophysiological and biomechanical levels (Figures 2 and 3), suggesting that glucose is a negative regulator of the maturation of fetal cardiomyocytes in vitro and in vivo, as well as a positive regulator of the mitotic activity of these cells.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Glucose is a negative regulator of the maturation of fetal cardiomyocytes in vitro and in vivo.
source: The results suggest that glucose deprivation induces cardiac maturation at genetic, morphological, metabolic, electrophysiological and biomechanical levels (Figures 2 and 3), suggesting that glucose is a negative regulator of the maturation of fetal cardiomyocytes in vitro and in vivo, as well as a positive regulator of the mitotic activity of these cells.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro hESC-CM data and in vivo diabetic pregnancy model data

claim: Glucose is a positive regulator of the mitotic activity of cardiomyocytes.
source: The results suggest that glucose deprivation induces cardiac maturation at genetic, morphological, metabolic, electrophysiological and biomechanical levels (Figures 2 and 3), suggesting that glucose is a negative regulator of the maturation of fetal cardiomyocytes in vitro and in vivo, as well as a positive regulator of the mitotic activity of these cells.
evidence: Supported by proliferation data in Figures 2, 5, and 7

claim: Perturbation of natural glucose starvation results in higher mitotic activity and lower maturity of cardiomyocytes in vivo.
source: Perturbation of the natural glucose starvation results in higher mitotic activity and lower maturity of cardiomyocytes in vivo (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by Akita mouse model data shown in Figure 7

claim: The metabolic switch during perinatal stages is necessary not only to meet the energy demand but also to induce the genetic program that facilitates the maturation of cardiomyocytes in vivo.
source: Together, our results suggest that the metabolic switch during perinatal stages is necessary not only to meet the energy demand but also to induce the genetic program that facilitates the maturation of the cardiomyocytes in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo data showing glucose effects on maturation

claim: Nucleotide biosynthesis via the PPP is the key regulator of the pro-mitotic/anti-maturation effect of glucose.
source: In our hESC-CM experiments, blocking the PPP and nucleotide biosynthesis inhibited the glucose-mediated induction of mitosis and suppression of maturation, and supplementation of nucleotides was sufficient to recapitulate the effect of glucose (Figures 4 and 5). These data suggest that nucleotide biosynthesis via the PPP is the key regulator of the pro-mitotic/anti-maturation effect of glucose.
evidence: Supported by chemical inhibitor and nucleotide supplementation data shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: It is not the cell cycle in general but the nucleotides themselves that block cardiomyocyte maturation.
source: Interestingly, cardiomyocyte maturation was not fully induced by blocking of the cell cycle with a CDK4/6 inhibitor or paclitaxel, neither of which directly impact the nucleotide kinetics. Therefore, it is not the cell cycle in general but the nucleotides themselves that blocks the maturation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by CDK4/6 inhibitor and paclitaxel treatment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: There is generally an inverse correlation between cell proliferation and differentiation during developmental stages.
source: It is well-documented that there is generally an inverse correlation between cell proliferation and differentiation during developmental stages (Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruijtenberg and van den Heuvel, 2016

claim: Nucleotide biosynthesis may serve as a nodal point balancing cell proliferation and differentiation during development.
source: Our data raise an intriguing possibility that nucleotide biosynthesis serves as a nodal point balancing cell proliferation and differentiation during development.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the experimental data

claim: Environmental glucose itself, if excessive, directly impacts cardiac differentiation.
source: To our knowledge, our in vitro study is the first to demonstrate that environmental glucose itself, if excessive, directly impacts cardiac differentiation.
evidence: Supported by in vitro hESC-CM experiments throughout the manuscript

claim: The glucose metabolic environment is both a consequence of changes in cardiac genetic program and a cause of changes in cardiac gene expression.
source: Our data suggest that the glucose metabolic environment is, on the one hand, a consequence of changes in cardiac genetic program, and on the other hand, a cause of the changes in cardiac gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from the bidirectional relationship observed between glucose metabolism and cardiac maturation

claim: 60 million women of reproductive age worldwide have diabetes mellitus.
source: Currently, 60 million women of reproductive age (18–44 years old) worldwide and approximately 3 million in the U.S. have diabetes mellitus.
evidence: Statistical data about diabetes prevalence

claim: The number of women of reproductive age with diabetes mellitus is predicted to double by 2030.
source: This number is predicted to double by 2030, posing a huge medical and economic burden (Gabbay-Benziv et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gabbay-Benziv et al., 2015

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation is low until E10.5 of developing rodent hearts and rapidly increases between E10.5 and E14.5.
source: Oxidative phosphorylation is low until E10.5 of developing rodent hearts and rapidly increases between E10.5 and E14.5 (Cox and Gunberg, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cox and Gunberg, 1972

claim: Rapid increase in oxidative phosphorylation coincides with rapid maturation of mitochondrial structure in embryonic cardiomyocytes.
source: This coincides with the rapid maturation of the mitochondrial structure in embryonic cardiomyocytes (Mackler et al., 1971).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mackler et al., 1971

claim: Shortly after birth, fatty acid oxidation becomes the predominant source of ATP production in the heart.
source: Shortly after birth, fatty acid oxidation becomes the predominant source of ATP production to meet the high energy demand of the maturing heart (Warshaw and Terry, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warshaw and Terry, 1970

claim: Akita heterozygous mice carry a single amino-acid substitution in the Ins2 gene and exhibit multiple disorders associated with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY).
source: Akita heterozygous mice carry a single amino-acid substitution in the Ins2 gene and exhibit multiple disorders associated with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) (Barber et al., 2005; Fujita et al., 2001; Wang et al., 1999; Yaguchi et al., 2003; Yoshioka et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barber et al., 2005; Fujita et al., 2001; Wang et al., 1999; Yaguchi et al., 2003; Yoshioka et al., 1997

claim: The number of CHD patients who survive childhood is growing rapidly by nearly 5% per year.
source: With the advances in fetal diagnosis and surgical techniques, the number of CHD patients who survive childhood (and so have adult CHD) is growing rapidly by nearly 5% per year (Brickner et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brickner et al., 2000
